Welcome to the Jumbo Hostel -- an old Boeing 747 which is being converted into a 25-room hostel at the Stockholm-Arlanda airport. Renovation work is underway on a plane which used to carry in excess of 350 passengers. "We were looking to expand the business but it was more or less impossible to find reasonably priced housing at the airport. And you cannot build a new house and run a hostel because it is too expensive," he said. It was in 2006 that Dios first heard about the Boeing 747, which was for sale. Formerly flown by the now defunct Transjet Airways, the plane was wasting away in a hangar at Arlanda airport and hadn't flown since 2002. "The plane was in a terrible state when we first saw it," he said. "But we contacted the owners and gave them a fairly good offer, I think." Dios took possession of the 1976 Boeing 747-200 -- one of 393 built by the company until 1991 -- in June 2007 and by December he had reached agreement with the airport authorities about his unique proposal. In August 2008 the plane was finally moved to its permanent home at Arlanda airport's main entrance, where it will now stay. Apart from the engines being removed from the wings before purchase, the plane, from the outside, looks almost exactly as it did when it was grounded. The interior, for obvious reasons, is a different matter. Dismantling and stripping out all the old equipment and instruments started earlier this year. The final phase of refurbishment is nearing completion and Dios says it complies with the same building regulations required for a house. There will be two types of accommodation. A basic room will be roughly six square meters in size with sleeping space for three adults. It will cost €110 ($150) per night. But if you fancy splashing out, you can book the top deck, complete with the cockpit suite, which comes with a private bathroom and panoramic views of takeoffs and landings. Dios envisages newlyweds taking advantage of this more expensive option, which costs €500 ($700). # Sleep on a jumbo jet: Inside Stockholm’s Boeing 747 hostel

**Stockholm, Sweden —** For travelers who have ever wished a long-haul flight could end with a proper bed, Stockholm-Arlanda Airport offers an unusual answer: a retired Boeing 747 converted into a hostel.

Known as **Jumbo Hostel** — now often marketed as **Jumbo Stay** — the aircraft sits just outside Sweden’s busiest airport, offering guests the chance to sleep inside one of aviation’s most recognizable planes without ever leaving the ground.

The project was the brainchild of **Oscar Dios**, a Swedish entrepreneur who saw an opportunity in a decommissioned jumbo jet and imagined a new kind of airport accommodation: part hostel, part aviation attraction.

Dios acquired the aircraft in the mid-2000s, and the extensive conversion work took place over roughly **2008**, with the hostel opening to guests around **early 2009**. The renovation transformed the jet’s cabin into compact rooms while preserving much of the novelty of being inside a Boeing 747 — including access to the cockpit area, which became one of the property’s most sought-after rooms.

## A 747 with beds instead of seats

The aircraft, a **Boeing 747-200**, once carried hundreds of passengers across continents. Today, it has around **33 rooms** and space for roughly **76 guests**, depending on room configuration.

Accommodation ranges from budget dormitory-style rooms with shared bathrooms to private rooms, with the standout option being the **cockpit suite**, where guests can sleep beneath the original flight controls and look out through the pilots’ windows.

Prices have varied over the years and by season, but the concept has typically offered budget beds from around **$50 per night**, with private rooms costing more and the cockpit suite commanding a premium — often several hundred dollars a night.

Bathrooms and showers are installed in the aircraft and in adjoining facilities, while a café and common areas cater to guests and curious visitors. The jet’s wings and exterior also provide popular photo opportunities, especially for aviation enthusiasts passing through Arlanda.

## From aviation relic to airport landmark

Converting a jumbo jet into accommodation was not as simple as removing seats and adding mattresses. The renovation required insulation, plumbing, electrical systems, ventilation, fire safety measures and adaptations to meet hospitality standards — all within the narrow, curved structure of an aircraft fuselage.

The result is a property that functions both as a practical airport hotel and a tourist attraction. Its location near Stockholm-Arlanda makes it especially convenient for travelers with early departures, late arrivals or long layovers.

For Dios, the appeal was in giving an aircraft a second life rather than letting it be dismantled for parts.

## Part of a wider trend

Jumbo Hostel is not the only example of aircraft being repurposed after retirement. Around the world, old planes have been turned into hotels, restaurants, homes and museums.

Among the better-known examples:

- **Hotel Costa Verde’s 727 Fuselage Suite in Costa Rica**, where a retired Boeing 727 has been converted into a luxury jungle accommodation overlooking the Pacific.
- **Vliegtuigsuite in the Netherlands**, a former Ilyushin aircraft transformed into a high-end private suite near Teuge Airport.
- **El Avion in Costa Rica**, a restaurant built around a Fairchild C-123 cargo plane.
- Various retired aircraft used as cafés, training centers, museum exhibits and themed rentals across Europe, North America and Asia.

The appeal is easy to understand: aircraft are expensive, highly engineered machines with powerful cultural associations. When their flying days end, their distinctive shapes and histories can still draw crowds.

## A stay for aviation fans — and curious travelers

For some guests, Jumbo Hostel is a budget-friendly airport stopover. For others, it is the chance to spend a night inside a queen of the skies — one of the aircraft that helped define the jet age.

Either way, the grounded jumbo at Stockholm-Arlanda has become more than a place to sleep. It is a reminder that even after an aircraft’s final landing, its journey may not be over.

## A jumbo with a long flying history

The aircraft used for Jumbo Stay is a **Boeing 747-200**, part of the early generation of jumbo jets that helped define long-haul air travel in the 1970s and 1980s. The plane was built in the mid-1970s and originally entered service with **Singapore Airlines**, one of the carriers that used the 747 to expand intercontinental routes during the golden age of wide-body aviation.

Over the following decades, the jet changed hands several times, flying for different operators before ending its active life in Sweden. Its final airline operator was connected to the Swedish carrier **Transjet**, which ceased operations in the early 2000s. After that, the aircraft remained at Arlanda, too costly to return to service but too distinctive to disappear unnoticed.

Diös acquired the aircraft and began converting it into accommodation. The conversion required extensive work: seats were removed, the cabin was reconfigured, plumbing and electrical systems were installed, insulation was improved for the Swedish climate, and fire-safety systems were added to meet hotel standards. The aircraft was placed on a permanent concrete foundation near the airport entrance, making it visible to arriving and departing passengers.

Jumbo Stay opened to guests in **2009**.

## Sleeping in economy, business — or the cockpit

Inside, the aircraft has been divided into compact guest rooms. Depending on configuration, the hostel offers roughly **30 rooms** and space for more than **70 guests**. Some rooms are built into the main passenger deck, while other areas of the aircraft have been adapted into showers, common spaces and a café-style reception area.

The most affordable option is a dormitory-style bed, aimed at backpackers, plane spotters and passengers with early flights. Prices have varied over the years, but budget beds have typically started at around **350 to 500 Swedish kronor** per night, depending on season and booking conditions.

Private rooms cost more, with standard twin or family rooms often priced in the range of **900 to 1,500 kronor** per night. Rooms with private bathrooms are generally higher.

The showpiece is the **cockpit suite**, located in the aircraft’s original flight deck. Guests sleeping there can look out through the cockpit windows across the airport area, with the captain’s and first officer’s controls still forming part of the setting. The cockpit suite has usually been marketed as the premium room, with prices commonly around **3,000 to 3,500 Swedish kronor** per night, and sometimes higher depending on demand.

The aircraft’s upper deck — once an exclusive space on many 747s — has also been converted for guests. Some of the most popular rooms are located there because of the novelty of sleeping in one of the most famous sections of a jumbo jet.

## From transport machine to destination

The hostel’s appeal lies partly in its contrast: the 747 was designed to move hundreds of people across continents, but at Jumbo Stay, the aircraft never leaves the ground. Travelers who once might have rushed through airports now check in simply to spend the night inside an aviation landmark.

The project also reflects a broader trend in adaptive reuse — finding second lives for industrial objects and transportation relics. Retired aircraft are difficult and expensive to preserve. They are large, complex structures that deteriorate quickly if left outdoors. Many are broken up for aluminum, engines, avionics and spare parts. Converting one into lodging allows the aircraft to remain intact while generating revenue.

For airports, such projects can also become tourist attractions. Jumbo Stay’s location near Arlanda gives it a built-in audience: transit passengers, aviation fans, families with children, and travelers who want accommodation close to terminals without choosing a conventional airport hotel.

## Other recycled aircraft projects

Jumbo Stay is not the only example of an aircraft repurposed into hospitality or leisure space, but its use of a Boeing 747 makes it one of the most dramatic.

In **Costa Rica**, the well-known **727 Fuselage Home** at Hotel Costa Verde uses a retired **Boeing 727** mounted in the jungle canopy near Manuel Antonio National Park. Unlike Jumbo Stay, which functions as a multi-room hostel, the Costa Rican aircraft is operated as a private luxury rental suite, with wood-paneled interiors and views over the forest and ocean.

In the **Netherlands**, the **Airplane Suite** at Teuge Airport converted a vintage **Ilyushin Il-18** airliner into a luxury hotel suite. That project emphasizes exclusivity, offering an entire aircraft for a private stay, complete with sauna and high-end furnishings.

In **New Zealand**, the **Woodlyn Park** motel complex near Waitomo has used a retired aircraft as part of a collection of unusual accommodations, alongside converted railway cars and other themed lodgings. The concept is similar in spirit: transportation equipment turned into overnight accommodation.

Other retired aircraft have become restaurants, classrooms, museums, event spaces and even homes. In the United States and Europe, former military and commercial aircraft have been converted into diners or roadside attractions. Some airports have preserved aircraft as viewing platforms or educational exhibits. But few projects have matched Jumbo Stay’s combination of scale, accessibility and aviation nostalgia.

## A symbol of aviation’s past and reuse

The Boeing 747 itself adds significance to the Swedish hostel. Introduced in 1970, the 747 revolutionized air travel by carrying more passengers farther and more economically than earlier jetliners. Its distinctive hump-backed upper deck made it instantly recognizable. For decades, it served as the flagship aircraft for major airlines.

As airlines retire older 747s in favor of more fuel-efficient twin-engine jets, many of the once-dominant jumbos have vanished from passenger service. Jumbo Stay preserves one of them in an unusual but practical way.

For Diös, the project was both a business venture and a preservation effort. Instead of leaving the aircraft to decay, he turned it into a functioning hostel that continues to attract attention from around the world.

Guests do not need a boarding pass to enter, and the aircraft will not be pushing back from the gate again. But for travelers checking into Jumbo Stay, the experience still carries some of the romance of long-haul flight — the chance to climb aboard a 747, settle in for the night and wake up beside one of Europe’s busiest airports inside a piece of aviation history.
